newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Bruton, Major, urge breakthrough at N.Ireland talks.
newsitem.headline: Bruton, Major, urge breakthrough at N.Ireland talks.

text.p: Britain and Ireland called on Northern Ireland's squabbling political parties on Saturday to compromise and begin real negotiations at Belfast peace talks threatened by guerrilla violence and political stalemate.

The Irish and British Prime Ministers, John Bruton and John Major, "agreed on the need to move speedily forward to substantial talks" at a series of meetings they held at a one- day European Union summit, an Irish spokesman said.

"Parties must show a willingness to compromise," the spokesman quoted the two premiers as saying after Bruton and Major discussed the Anglo-Irish peace process, which was launched almost two years ago.

They named no parties but the language appeared directed at both pro-British Protestant Unionist parties and pro-Irish nationalist groups who have clung on to entrenched positions since the talks started in June.
The issue of disarming rival guerrilla groups has dogged the peace process from day one and attempts by the two governments to find a compromise have fallen foul of both sides.
Irish officials fear that the talks may themselves be consigned to history unless there is a breakthrough in coming weeks.
The talks have failed to address a single substantive issue such as Northern Ireland's constitutional status since they opened under the chairmanship of former U.S. Senator George Mitchell in June.
Ulster Unionists, whose voters in the Protestant majority want the province to remain for ever British, insist that guerrilla groups must discuss disarmament as the first item on the agenda.
But the IRA, excluded from the negotiations as punishment for ending a 17-month ceasefire, says it will not hand over a single bullet until a political settlement is reached.
Unionists fear the two governments will try to ease the terms on disarmament to persuade the IRA to call a new truce which would allow its political wing, Sinn Fein, a seat at the talks.

The British and Irish governments have suggested that guerrillas might be allowed to disarm in stages as the talks progress but Unionists say this would allow their rivals to negotiate while their guerrilla supporters are still armed.
Irish officials are also worried that pro-British Loyalist guerrillas might break a two-year-old ceasefire.
Sources close to the Loyalists said at the weekend that a review of their policies would be made in coming days and would not rule out the possibility of the truce breaking down.
Loyalists are incensed that they have not been rewarded for maintaining their ceasefire by the release of hundreds of jailed activists.
Britain insists there can be no amnesty for anyone and rejects claims by both the IRA and the Loyalists that such activists are political prisoners.
